1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.
6	
7	Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.
8	
9	Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.
10	
11	The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.
12	
13	Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.
14	
15	Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.
16	
17	The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.
18

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

The present invention relates to a vibration device for setting tiles and other covering materials into thinset, mortar, adhesive, or similar bonding material. Conventional tile vibrators generally include a vibrating motor connected to a handle and either a smooth sliding base or a flexible suction cup. The vibration is intended to remove trapped air, distribute the bonding material, improve surface contact, and strengthen the bond between the tile and the underlying substrate.

Existing systems have two main disadvantages. First, vibration from the motor is not efficiently coupled to the tile. A smooth sliding base must be pressed firmly against the tile by the operator, and even then a thin layer of air between the base and the tile may dampen vibration transfer. A suction-cup system creates a stronger connection, but the flexible rubber or foam forming the suction cup absorbs and dampens part of the vibration. A conventional suction cup also attaches the machine at one fixed location, preventing it from sliding across the tile and causing vibration intensity to decrease at areas farther from the attachment point.

Second, existing systems require the operator to continuously apply substantial downward pressure to maintain contact with the tile. This transfers vibration into the operator’s hands, wrists, arms, and joints, creating discomfort, fatigue, and possible injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles may reduce some vibration reaching the operator, but they also absorb mechanical energy that could otherwise be transferred to the tile. Furthermore, stronger coupling generally requires greater hand pressure, which increases the vibration experienced by the operator.

The invention addresses these problems by providing a vibration motor coupled to a first side of a rigid base. An air-extraction mechanism, such as a vacuum pump, is also coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber located on a second side of the base. The perimeter of the second side is formed as a rigid loop or skirt made from a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, PTFE, or a combination of rigid materials.

Unlike conventional vacuum grippers or suction cups, the rigid perimeter is not intended to form a complete airtight seal and does not rely on flexible rubber or foam. Instead, it restricts airflow into the chamber while maintaining rigid contact with the tile. The air-extraction mechanism continuously removes air entering beneath the rigid perimeter, maintaining the chamber at a lower pressure than the surrounding atmosphere. The resulting pressure differential holds the device firmly against the tile without requiring the operator to press downward.

Because the vibration motor is connected to the tile through rigid components, vibration energy is transferred with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. At the same time, the low-friction perimeter allows the device to slide freely across different areas of the tile while the vacuum continuously maintains contact.

The device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding the machine rather than pressing it against the surface. In another embodiment, a rope, wire, cable, or similar flexible pulling element is connected to the device. Pulling the flexible element moves the device across the tile, while the pressure differential independently supplies the force holding the device against the surface. This provides decoupled control in which the operator controls position using minimal pulling force while the vacuum maintains consistent coupling and vibration transfer. The invention therefore maximizes vibration delivered to the tile while minimizing vibration, pressure, fatigue, and joint stress experienced by the operator.

1	In the following description, the same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings. The embodiments described are examples and do not limit the scope of what is claimed.
2	
3	Overview
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a vibration device 10 in use, FIG. 2 shows it in vertical section, and FIG. 4 shows the bedded layers beneath it in enlarged detail. A covering element 36, which may be a tile or other covering material, has been laid onto a bed of bonding material 40 spread over a substrate 42, as seen in FIG. 4. The bonding material 40 may be thinset, mortar, tile adhesive or any similar bonding material. The substrate 42 is the surface being covered. The covering element 36 presents an exposed face 38 facing away from the bonding material 40. The vibration device 10 rests on the exposed face 38 and delivers vibration into the covering element 36, which drives trapped air out of the bonding material 40, distributes the bonding material 40 more evenly beneath the covering element 36, increases the area of contact between the covering element 36 and the bonding material 40, and strengthens the bond between the covering element 36 and the substrate 42.
6	
7	The vibration device 10 comprises a base 12, a vibration motor 18, an air-extraction mechanism 20 and a perimeter member 24. The base 12 is rigid and has a first side 14 facing away from the covering element 36 and a second side 16 opposite the first side 14 and facing the covering element 36. The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14. The air-extraction mechanism 20 is also coupled to the first side 14 and is in fluid communication with a chamber 22 located on the second side 16. The perimeter member 24 extends from the second side 16 around the chamber 22 and terminates in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38.
8	
9	The base
10	
11	The base 12 is rigid: under the alternating force produced by the vibration motor 18 and under the pressure differential described below, the base 12 is not compliant, and it transmits the vibration to the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than a flexible suction cup would.
12	
13	The second side 16 of the base 12 forms the upper boundary of the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is in fluid communication with the air-extraction mechanism 20.
14	
15	The vibration motor
16	
17	The vibration motor 18 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, with no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount interposed between the vibration motor 18 and the base 12. That direct coupling is intentional. A resilient motor mount would isolate the base 12 from the vibration motor 18, which is the opposite of what is wanted: the entire object of the device is to put vibration into the covering element 36, and any compliant member anywhere between the vibration motor 18 and the exposed face 38 removes energy from that transfer.
18	
19	The vibration motor 18 produces mechanical vibration in the base 12.
20	
21	The air-extraction mechanism
22	
23	The air-extraction mechanism 20 is coupled to the first side 14 of the base 12, as seen in FIG. 2, and withdraws air from the chamber 22. In the embodiment shown, the air-extraction mechanism 20 is a vacuum pump carried on the base 12.
24	
25	The air-extraction mechanism 20 runs continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. It is not run to establish a vacuum and then stopped: the chamber 22 is never sealed, so the pressure differential exists only while the air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22.
26	
27	The perimeter member and the chamber
28	
29	A perimeter member 24 stands proud of the second side 16 and surrounds the chamber 22: a rigid loop, or skirt, that runs round the second side 16 at its perimeter. As shown in FIG. 3, the perimeter member 24 is a closed loop running around the second side 16 at its perimeter. The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.
30	
31	The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.
32	
33	The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.
34	
35	Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.
36	
37	The pressure differential that holds the device down
38	
39	The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.
40	
41	The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.
42	
43	The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.
44	
45	The vibration transmission path
46	
47	The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.
48	
49	The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.
50	
51	The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.
52	
53	The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.
54	
55	Handles
56	
57	The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.
58	
59	Embodiment with a flexible pulling element
60	
61	FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.
62	
63	This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.
64	
65	Method of use
66	
67	A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.
68

The perimeter member 24, the second side 16 of the base 12 and, in use, the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36 together bound the chamber 22. The chamber 22 is a single space bounded by one perimeter member 24, as shown in FIG. 2. The perimeter member 24 is rigidly connected to the base 12 at the second side 16, and vibration passes from the base 12 into the perimeter member 24 with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup.

The perimeter member 24 terminates, at its end remote from the base 12, in a bearing face 26 that contacts the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. The perimeter member 24 is made of a low-friction rigid material, and the bearing face 26 is the end face of that member, so that the face bearing on the exposed face 38 is of that low-friction material. Suitable materials are plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), and combinations of rigid materials.

The perimeter member 24 is not a seal. It is free of rubber, elastomer and foam. This distinguishes it from a suction cup and from a compliant sealing skirt, and the difference is functional rather than nominal. A suction cup works by conforming to the surface, closing the enclosed space against the atmosphere, and holding the reduced pressure inside; conforming requires compliance, and compliance in the load path damps vibration. The perimeter member 24 is instead hard and dimensionally stable, and it makes rigid contact with the exposed face 38.

Because the perimeter member 24 is not intended to form a complete airtight seal, a clearance 34 remains between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38 along at least part of the perimeter member 24, as shown enlarged in FIG. 4, which is an enlarged fragmentary detail of the lower end of the perimeter member 24, taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 where the clearance 34 is present. The clearance 34 is shown enlarged for clarity. FIG. 2 is taken through places along the perimeter member 24 at which the perimeter member 24 bears on the covering element 36, and FIG. 4 is taken at a place along the perimeter member 24 at which the clearance 34 is present. The enlarged detail of FIG. 4 also shows the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, and the covering element 36 bedded in the bonding material 40 that has been spread over the substrate 42. Ambient air passes through the clearance 34 into the chamber 22 continuously while the vibration device 10 is in use. The clearance 34 is not a defect to be eliminated. It is the condition the vibration device 10 is designed to work in: the perimeter member 24 restricts the flow of ambient air into the chamber 22 without closing that path.

The pressure differential that holds the device down

The air-extraction mechanism 20 withdraws air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance 34, for as long as the air-extraction mechanism 20 runs.

The difference between atmospheric pressure and the pressure in the chamber 22, acting over the plan area of the chamber 22, produces a holding force that presses the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The holding force is sufficient to hold the vibration device 10 against the exposed face 38 without any downward force being applied by an operator. The contact load is therefore supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator's hands.

The vibration device 10 can be translated across the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is being maintained. The pressure differential is maintained continuously throughout the translating, so that the vibration device 10 is held against the covering element 36 and slid over the exposed face 38 at the same time; holding and sliding are simultaneous, not alternatives. The bearing face 26, being of a low-friction material, is slidable over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential is maintained, and the air-extraction mechanism 20 continues to run and continues to hold the vibration device 10 down throughout the movement. No grip has to be released and re-established. Vibration can therefore be delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36, instead of the vibration intensity falling away with distance from a single fixed attachment point.

The vibration transmission path

The vibration transmission path runs as follows. Vibration produced by the vibration motor 18 passes into the base 12 at the first side 14, along the base 12, into the perimeter member 24 at the second side 16, along the perimeter member 24, and out through the bearing face 26 into the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36. Every member in that path, namely the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 terminating in the bearing face 26, is rigid, and no elastomeric member, foam member or resilient mount is interposed anywhere along it. The vibration therefore reaches the covering element 36 with substantially less damping than it would in an arrangement in which a flexible suction cup, a resilient motor mount or a vibration-damping handle lies in the path.

The holding force from the pressure differential also acts to keep the bearing face 26 in contact with the exposed face 38. Contact is maintained by a force that does not vary with what the operator is doing, which is what makes the transfer consistent across the working area.

The clearance 34 does not separate the bearing face 26 from the covering element 36 over the whole of the loop, in the way that a film of air separates a pressed-on sliding base from the covering element beneath it. A sliding base of that kind is separated from the covering element over its whole area, so that everything crossing the interface must cross the film, and the film may dampen the vibration crossing it. Here the bearing face 26 is loaded onto the exposed face 38 by the holding force and bears rigidly on it, and the vibration is carried across that rigid contact. The clearance 34, present along at least part of the perimeter member 24, admits ambient air into the chamber 22 without the bearing face 26 being separated from the exposed face 38 by an intervening compliant member. Nothing compressible is interposed in the load path, and the holding force presses the contact together rather than holding the two faces apart.

The force balance on the vibration device 10 in use is as follows. The weight of the vibration device 10 and the holding force act downward on the covering element 36; the reaction of the exposed face 38 acts upward; the frictional resistance of the bearing face 26 acts in the plane of the exposed face 38 and opposes translation; and the force the operator need supply is an in-plane force sufficient to overcome that frictional resistance and to steer. Because no downward force is required from the operator, no loaded path need be maintained from the vibrating device into the operator's hands, wrists, arms and joints. The vibration reaching the operator is reduced not by absorbing it in a damper, which would take the same energy away from the covering element 36, but by removing the operator from the load path altogether. The usual trade-off, in which stronger coupling to the covering element 36 is bought with greater hand pressure and therefore with greater vibration exposure, does not arise here: the coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and the operator's grip has nothing to do with it.

Handles

The vibration device 10 may include one or more handles 44, as shown in FIG. 1. The handle 44 is arranged to guide the vibration device 10 over the exposed face 38 while the pressure differential holds the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36. The handle 44 serves primarily to guide the vibration device 10 rather than to press it against the covering element 36, because the contact load is supplied by the pressure differential.

Embodiment with a flexible pulling element

FIG. 5 shows a second embodiment. A flexible pulling element 46 is connected to the vibration device 10. The flexible pulling element 46 is a rope, wire, cable or similar flexible pulling element. The vibration device 10 is translatable over the exposed face 38 by tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46 while the pressure differential is maintained: the operator applies that tension and the vibration device 10 slides on the bearing face 26 in the direction of the applied tension.

This embodiment gives decoupled control. The flexible pulling element 46 moves the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38 when the operator applies tension to it. The force holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 is supplied independently, and continuously, by the pressure differential across the base 12. Position is thus controlled by one agency and contact by another: the operator sets where the vibration device 10 is with a small pulling force, while the quality of the vibration coupling is set by the air-extraction mechanism 20 and is supplied independently of the tension applied to the flexible pulling element 46.

Method of use

A method of bedding a covering element 36 into bonding material 40 using the vibration device 10 is carried out as follows. The method begins with placing the vibration device 10 on the exposed face 38 of the covering element 36, whereby the bearing face 26 of the perimeter member 24 is brought against the exposed face 38 so that the chamber 22 is bounded by the second side 16, the perimeter member 24 and the exposed face 38, with the clearance 34 remaining, along at least part of the perimeter member 24, between the bearing face 26 and the exposed face 38. It continues with operating the air-extraction mechanism 20 to withdraw air from the chamber 22 at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber 22 below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter the chamber 22 through the clearance 34, the resulting pressure differential holding the vibration device 10 against the covering element 36 without a downward force being required from the operator. It continues with operating the vibration motor 18 and transmitting vibration from the vibration motor 18 to the covering element 36 through the base 12 and the perimeter member 24 to the bearing face 26. It continues with translating the vibration device 10 across the exposed face 38, while the pressure differential is maintained, by sliding the bearing face 26 over the exposed face 38, so that vibration is delivered to successive areas of the covering element 36. The translating may be done by applying tension to the flexible pulling element 46, or by guiding the vibration device 10 with the handle 44.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area.

1	When a tile or similar covering element is laid onto a bed of thinset, mortar or adhesive, air is trapped between the covering element and the bonding material and the bonding material is unevenly distributed beneath the covering element. Mechanical vibration applied to the exposed face of the covering element after it is laid drives the trapped air out, spreads the bonding material into a more uniform layer, increases the area over which the bonding material actually touches the covering element, and thereby improves the strength of the completed bond. Hand-guided vibration devices are used for this purpose.
2	
3	Such devices generally comprise a vibration motor carried on a handle together with one of two arrangements for putting the vibration into the covering element: a smooth sliding base that the operator presses down onto the exposed face, or a flexible suction cup that grips the exposed face at one place. In one known hand-held device for lifting and laying tiles, a handle carries two shafts, an electric motor vibrates the shafts, and a head shell at the free end of each shaft carries a suction cup on its underside, the suction cups being evacuated by an electrically operated pump and each being formed by a rubber-elastic apron [REF:DE-202021002652-U1].
4	
5	Both arrangements couple the vibration into the covering element poorly. A smooth sliding base has to be pressed hard against the covering element by the operator, and even under that pressure a thin film of air can remain between the base and the covering element and damp the vibration crossing the interface. A flexible suction cup makes a firmer connection, but the rubber or foam wall that forms the cup is compliant, and a compliant member placed in the path between the motor and the covering element absorbs and dissipates part of the vibration instead of delivering it. A device gripped by such a cup is also anchored at one place on the covering element: it cannot be slid to another area without first releasing the grip, and the vibration amplitude reaching areas remote from the point of attachment falls off with distance from that point.
6	
7	The same reliance on a compliant wall, and the same treatment of holding and moving as alternatives, are found in vacuum coupling arrangements used away from tile setting. In one adhesion device that holds itself to a wall surface, the peripheral wall of the decompressed space between the base and the wall surface is formed by elastic partitions, of which the partition nearer the wall surface has an end that contacts the wall surface, and a frame member of higher rigidity is added on the partition to restrict the partition from being deformed into that space as it is drawn down [REF:US-11408462-B2]. In a base assembly for coupling an end effector to a structure, a cavity on the second side of the assembly is held to the structure by vacuum drawn by a pneumatic generator operating in a suction mode, and the assembly is moved across the structure substantially frictionlessly on an air cushion produced by the same generator operating in a blower mode [REF:US-10001245-B2], so that the vacuum coupling is given up for the period during which the assembly is moved. In a device that suction-adheres to a wall surface and moves along it, a seal member mounted in the main body defines a pressure reduction space in cooperation with the wall surface, vacuum creating means discharges fluid from that space so that the main body adheres by the difference in fluid pressure inside and outside the space, and vibration generating means mounted on the main body imparts a lifting force in a direction away from the wall surface that reduces the suction-adhering force, together with a force along the wall surface that moves the main body [REF:US-4934475-A]. The vibration there is used to loosen the suction-adhering hold and to drive the main body along the wall surface. Vacuum is used differently again in handling equipment, where the object is to pick a workpiece up rather than to hold a tool down on it: in one vacuum plate lifting system for lifting sheet material articles, a substantially horizontal suction plate has a perforated suction lifting surface directed downward for contact with the upper surface of the article, an airflow suction system conveys vacuum air pressure to that surface, a lifter actuation system such as a robotic arm lifts and moves the plate, and an elongate bar movably mounted along an edge of the plate carries nozzles that are lowered to sweep a suction airflow across the surface beneath to remove dust or debris [REF:US-11247858-B2]. That system carries the article away from the work surface and cleans the work surface by suction; it does not deliver vibration into a covering element already laid on a bed of bonding material, and it accordingly says nothing about how a vibrating tool might be kept in contact with such a covering element while it is moved over it.
8	
9	The second problem with existing tile vibration devices concerns the operator rather than the tile. Because contact has to be maintained by hand, the operator applies substantial and continuous downward force through the handle, and vibration travels back up that loaded path into the hands, wrists, arms and joints, producing discomfort, fatigue and a risk of injury. Shock absorbers and vibration-damping handles reduce some of the vibration reaching the operator, but they do so by absorbing mechanical energy that would otherwise have gone into the covering element, so the tool is made kinder to the operator by being made worse at its job. The two problems are coupled: firmer coupling to the covering element is obtained by pressing harder, and pressing harder is exactly what increases the vibration dose to the operator.
10	
11	What is needed is a way to hold a vibration device against a covering element with a force that does not come from the operator's arms, to conduct the vibration into the covering element without passing it through any compliant member, and to allow the device to be moved from area to area over the covering element without ever giving up that hold.
12

A rigid perimeter member of low-friction material such as plastic or PTFE surrounds the chamber, its end face forming a bearing face. 1	A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.
2	
3	The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.
4	
5	Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.
6	
7	Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.
8	
9	In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.
10	
11	A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.
12

A vibration device is disclosed for bedding a covering element into thinset, mortar, adhesive or similar bonding material. The device has a rigid base with a first side and a second side. A vibration motor is coupled to the first side. An air-extraction mechanism is coupled to the first side and is in fluid communication with a chamber on the second side. A perimeter member extends from the second side around the chamber and terminates in a bearing face that rests on the exposed face of the covering element. The perimeter member is rigid and of a low-friction material such as plastic, metal, polytetrafluoroethylene, or a combination of rigid materials, and the bearing face is the end face of that member.

The perimeter member is not a seal and is not asked to behave like one. When the bearing face rests on the exposed face, a clearance remains along at least part of the perimeter member through which ambient air passes continuously into the chamber. The perimeter member restricts that flow without stopping it. The air-extraction mechanism withdraws air from the chamber at a volumetric extraction rate sufficient to maintain the chamber below atmospheric pressure while ambient air continues to enter through the clearance. The resulting pressure differential acts over the area of the chamber and presses the device against the covering element.

Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the arrangement. First, the force holding the device down is supplied by the pressure differential rather than by the operator, so the operator need not press the device against the covering element, and the loaded, vibrating path from tool to hand is avoided rather than damped. Second, every member in the path from the vibration motor to the covering element, namely the base and the perimeter member terminating in the bearing face, is rigid, with no elastomeric or foam element interposed, so the vibration crosses into the covering element with substantially less damping than through a flexible suction cup. The device is thus coupled to the covering element without an intervening compliant member or air film, while the operator's hands carry less.

Because the member that touches the covering element is a rigid low-friction bearing face rather than a gripping cup, the device can be translated across the exposed face while the pressure differential is being maintained. Holding and sliding are not alternative modes to be switched between: the same continuously running extraction keeps the device down while it is moved, so vibration can be delivered at successive positions over the covering element without the hold ever being released and without the vibration amplitude falling away with distance from a fixed attachment point.

In one embodiment the device carries one or more handles, which serve to guide and steer the device rather than to press it down. In another embodiment a flexible pulling element such as a rope, wire or cable is attached to the device, and the operator moves the device by pulling on that element. This gives decoupled control: the position of the device is set by a small pulling force applied by the operator, while the force holding the device against the covering element, and with it the quality of the vibration coupling, is set independently and constantly by the pressure differential.

A method of bedding a covering element using the device, and a system comprising the device together with the flexible pulling element, are also disclosed.

# FIG. 1 - Perspective view of the vibration device in use

**View:** Perspective view from above and to the front left. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The covering element 36 is one large plain tile in perspective filling the lower drawing area, the machine standing on its left-hand part with open tile to the right.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. Slab, band, blocks and tile are shown schematically, these rectangular forms being a convention for this sheet only; the position of the handle 44 is a placement convention asserting no mounting location.

The slab is drawn thick, its front face turned toward the viewer as the largest surface of the machine and able to hold a point well clear of its boundary lines. Its right-hand end is one long straight edge between the top face and the band.

Each of the three blocks is drawn broad and tall, its front face turned toward the viewer as a large plain surface able to hold a point well clear of its boundary lines.

The band meets the underside of the slab and follows the same rectangular run, its front surface facing the viewer as one unbroken strip across the whole width, drawn deep enough for a point to stand well inside it; its depth is schematic and no proportion asserted. It stands on the tile, its lower edge meeting it.

The whole of the drawing stands well inside the drawing area, the machine drawn large within it.

- The vibration device 10 is the whole machine, slab, blocks and band together. Identified on the outer boundary line of the machine at the right-hand end of the slab, on that long straight edge and away from either of its ends.

- The vibration motor 18 is the left-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The air-extraction mechanism 20 is the right-hand block. Identified well inside its front face.
- The perimeter member 24 is the band beneath the slab. Identified well inside its front strip, clear of its upper and lower edges.
- The covering element 36 is the tile. Identified well inside the open tile to the right of the machine.
- The handle 44 is the middle block, standing between the other two. Identified well inside its front face, clear of all four of its boundary lines.

Both findings were inside the FIG. 1 brief; both are fixed there, and nothing else was touched.

- **Handle disclaimer contradiction**: the clause denying any mounting location while the same paragraph draws the handle 44 standing on the top face is replaced. The brief now says the side-by-side order and spacing of the three blocks is a placement convention for this sheet only, and that no particular handle form, size or mounting arrangement is asserted. The depicted contact and the disclaimer now describe the same convention instead of denying each other.
- **Relative-proportion assertion**: "the largest surface of the machine" is gone. The slab's front face is now specified only as a large plain surface able to hold a point clear of its boundary lines, with its proportions schematic and no proportion asserted, matching the treatment already given to the band and the three blocks on the same sheet.

Both edits keep the annotation requirement that each numeral needs a broad interior target, and neither adds or removes a body, numeral, contact or relationship. FIG. 1 still carries 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36 and 44, with 10 on the machine's outer boundary line at the right-hand end of the slab, matching FIG. 5. `draft/07-drawings.md` and the "Handles" paragraph of `draft/08-detailed-description.md` remain shape-neutral and location-neutral as the review found them, `draft/numerals.md` is unchanged and still closes in both directions, and the claims are untouched. A scan of `draft/` and `figures/` finds no comparative-size wording, no person-directed text, no placeholder or note, and no em dash.

input.summary: Fixed both review findings, which were confined to figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md. The handle placement disclaimer no longer contradicts the geometry it accompanies: it now disclaims the side-by-side order and spacing of the three blocks and any particular handle form, size or mounting arrangement, rather than denying the mounting relationship the same paragraph draws. The unsourced comparative size claim that the base front face is the largest surface of the machine is replaced by the annotation requirement alone, a large plain surface able to hold a point clear of its boundary lines, with proportions stated as schematic in line with every other body on the sheet. No claim, description, drawing description, numeral table entry or other figure brief was changed, and no body, numeral, contact or relationship was added or removed.
reasoning: Both defects were annotation and convention wording inside one figure brief, not invention content, so the repair stayed inside that file. The disclosure says only that the device may include one or more handles used primarily for guiding rather than pressing, and gives no attachment point, so the sheet has to adopt some placement while the brief says plainly that the placement is a drawing convention. The old wording tried to disclaim the mounting relationship itself, which the same paragraph then drew; the new wording disclaims the particulars actually chosen, so the convention and the geometry now agree.

The comparative claim that the base front face was the largest surface of the machine asserted a size relationship between the base and the vibration motor, handle and air-extraction mechanism that the disclosure nowhere supplies; it only says the motor and the air-extraction mechanism are coupled to a first side of a rigid base. Only the annotation need is legitimate, namely a surface broad enough to hold a numeral endpoint clear of its edges, and that is now all the brief asks for.

Adding the explicit schematic-proportion statement to the slab brings it into line with the band and the three blocks on the same sheet, so the whole sheet asserts no proportion anywhere and the internal inconsistency the check found disappears.

I preserved the numeral endpoint targets as broad interior targets: base 12 well inside its front face clear of all four boundary lines, and each block well inside its front face. Those remain workable because the annotation requirement survived the edit intact; removing the comparative claim does not shrink any surface.

I left the assembly numeral 10 on the machine's outer boundary line at the right-hand end of the slab, on the long straight edge and away from either of its ends. That is the convention FIG. 5 was brought into line with last turn, and the qualifier is necessary there to keep 10 off the front face that carries base 12 rather than being an aesthetic coordinate.

Nothing in the application text needed to move. The review confirmed draft/07-drawings.md says only that the handle is shown schematically and the Handles paragraph of the detailed description assigns the handle no location, so the text was already free of the defect and rewriting it would have risked passing material.

No generated image was allowed to influence the text. The edits only remove an unsourced proportion and repair a self-contradictory convention statement; no shape, size, placement or embodiment was added to the specification, claims or numeral table.

Re-verified the file-level state after editing: draft/numerals.md still holds 16 numerals, one part name each, closing in both directions against the text; sheet assignments are unchanged at FIG. 1 with 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44, FIG. 2 with 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36, FIG. 3 with 16, 24, FIG. 4 with 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 and FIG. 5 with 10, 24, 36, 46, none over eight; and no comparative-size wording, person-directed text, placeholder or em dash remains anywhere in draft/ or figures/.

Claim scope is untouched and rests where it did: claim 1 pairs a rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately leaves a clearance admitting ambient air with extraction fast enough to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure and an all-rigid path to a bearing face that stays slidable while the differential is maintained, which is what separates it from the compliant-walled and mode-switching vacuum arrangements in the references.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the repair touched only figure-brief convention wording. Claim 1 recites a rigid, low-friction perimeter member that is expressly not a seal, with a clearance remaining along at least part of it through which ambient air continues to enter the chamber, extraction at a volumetric rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure during that inflow, an all-rigid vibration path from motor through base and perimeter member to the bearing face with no elastomeric, foam or resilient member interposed, and a bearing face that stays slidable while the differential is maintained. US-11408462-B2 builds its peripheral wall from elastic partitions whose end contacts the wall surface and adds a rigid frame member to stop that partition deforming inward, so it teaches the compliant wall this claim excludes from the load path. DE-202021002652-U1 evacuates rubber-elastic aprons on head shells at the ends of motor-vibrated shafts, an anchored compliant cup rather than a rigid leaking bearing loop. US-10001245-B2 holds by vacuum and then switches the same pneumatic generator to blower mode to float the assembly on an air cushion for movement, alternating hold and move where the claim requires the hold to persist through sliding contact. US-4934475-A defines its pressure reduction space with a seal member and uses vibration to impart a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering hold, the opposite role vibration plays here. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction plate that lifts sheet articles and sweeps debris with nozzle airflow, cited in the Background for that supported teaching and for saying nothing about keeping a vibrating tool on a covering element already bedded in bonding material. The Background states the technical problem the deliberate clearance solves, that sealing demands compliance and compliance in the load path damps the vibration.

The machine is one plain rectangular slab, the base 12, standing on a band that runs round its underside. Three closed blocks stand side by side on the top face of the slab: the left-hand block is the vibration motor 18, the middle block is the handle 44, and the right-hand block is the air-extraction mechanism 20. content.text:
The mechanical check listed one sheet: FIG. 1, numeral 10's terminal dot landing on the machine outline at the left end of the slab rather than on the long far edge at the right-hand end that the brief named.

The brief was asking for a target this view hides. FIG. 1 is taken from above and the front left, so the end of the slab presented to the viewer is the left-hand one; the right-hand end is the far side of the machine, seen only as a foreshortened silhouette behind the blocks. I moved the target for the assembly numeral to the outline the view actually shows and made it a broad run rather than a point:

- `figures/FIG-1-PERSPECTIVE-VIEW-OF-THE-VIBRATION-DEVICE-IN-USE.md`, geometry: the sentence defining the right-hand end as the long straight edge is replaced by one stating that, the view being from the front left, the left-hand end of the slab is also presented to the viewer and the machine's outline there stands upright from the band up to the top face of the slab.
- Same file, numeral list: numeral 10 is now identified on that upright outline at the left-hand end of the slab, anywhere along it between the band below and the top face above, and clear of the front face of the slab. The "away from either of its ends" modifier is gone, so the endpoint is a broad interior run on the intended line instead of a narrow spot.

The one restriction kept, clear of the front face of the slab, is the distinction that keeps 10 from landing on the surface FIG. 1 labels as base 12; every other sheet convention is untouched. FIG. 1 still carries 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36 and 44, and the assembly numeral still rides the machine outline rather than any face that carries its own numeral, which is the same convention FIG. 5 uses. No claim, description, drawing description, numeral table entry or other figure file was changed, and no geometry, part or relationship was added, removed or resized.

input.summary: Repaired the one failing sheet, FIG. 1, where the terminal dot for numeral 10 fell on the machine outline at the left end of the slab instead of the far right-hand edge the brief named. The brief had specified a target that this viewpoint does not present: the view is taken from above and the front left, so the left-hand end of the slab faces the viewer while the right-hand end is the far silhouette. The geometry paragraph now describes the upright outline at the left-hand end that this view shows, and numeral 10 is identified anywhere along that upright outline between the band below and the top face of the slab above, clear of the front face of the slab. The toward-an-end modifier was removed so the endpoint is a broad run on the intended line. No other figure, and no claim, description, drawing description or numeral table entry, was changed.
reasoning: The failure was a mismatch inside the figure brief, not a defect in the invention: FIG. 1 is drawn from above and the front left, which presents the front face and the left-hand end of the slab, while the brief pointed the assembly numeral at the right-hand end, the far side of the machine that this view foreshortens and the blocks partly stand in front of. Naming the outline the view actually presents removes the conflict at its source rather than restating the same instruction more loudly.

I kept the assembly numeral on the machine outline rather than moving it onto any face. Every visible surface on this sheet already belongs to a numbered part, the slab front face to base 12, the three blocks to vibration motor 18, handle 44 and air-extraction mechanism 20, and the band to perimeter member 24, so the outline is the only place where 10 can denote the whole machine without reading as one of its parts. That is also the convention FIG. 5 uses, so the two sheets stay consistent.

Following the endpoint guidance, I widened the target instead of narrowing it: the dot may fall anywhere along the upright outline between the band below and the top face above. I deleted the modifier requiring it to sit away from either end of the edge, which was an aesthetic coordinate with no grounding in the disclosure.

The single restriction I kept, clear of the front face of the slab, is retained because it is necessary to distinguish the whole machine from base 12, the part whose own endpoint sits well inside that face. That distinction was the subject of an earlier finding about the same surface reading as two numerals, and it still holds.

I used explicit left and right terms tied to the stated viewing direction rather than an ordinal that could be read from either side, and I anchored the run between two named bodies, the band below and the top face above, so the line is identifiable without counting strokes or measuring.

I did not touch FIG. 5, which passed inspection this round. Its numeral 10 sits on the machine outline clear of the flexible pulling element 46 that meets the machine on the left, and editing a passing sheet to match a cosmetic detail of another sheet would risk a regression for no gain in the convention, which is outline rather than face on both.

Nothing in the application text depends on which edge carries a leader. draft/07-drawings.md describes FIG. 1 only as a perspective view with the parts shown schematically, and the detailed description assigns the handle no location, so no text needed to move and none was moved. No shape, proportion or placement from any rendered sheet was allowed into the specification, claims or numeral table.

Post-edit state re-verified: draft/numerals.md still lists 16 numerals, one part name each; sheet assignments are unchanged at FIG. 1 with 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44, FIG. 2 with 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36, FIG. 3 with 16, 24, FIG. 4 with 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42 and FIG. 5 with 10, 24, 36, 46, none exceeding eight; and no note, placeholder, question, person-directed text or em dash appears in draft/ or figures/.

Claim scope is untouched. Claim 1 still turns on the rigid low-friction perimeter member that deliberately leaves a clearance admitting ambient air, extraction fast enough to hold the chamber below atmospheric pressure during that inflow, an all-rigid path from motor to bearing face, and a bearing face that stays slidable while the differential is maintained.

input.prior_art_strategy: Unchanged this turn; the repair touched only a leader target in one figure brief. Claim 1 recites a rigid, low-friction perimeter member that is expressly not a seal, a clearance remaining along at least part of it through which ambient air continues to enter the chamber, extraction at a volumetric rate sufficient to keep the chamber below atmospheric pressure during that inflow, an all-rigid vibration path from motor through base and perimeter member to the bearing face with no elastomeric, foam or resilient member interposed, and a bearing face slidable over the exposed face while the differential is maintained. US-11408462-B2 forms its peripheral wall from elastic partitions whose end contacts the wall surface and adds a rigid frame member to stop that partition deforming into the decompressed space, teaching the compliant wall this claim excludes from the load path. DE-202021002652-U1 evacuates rubber-elastic aprons on head shells at the ends of motor-vibrated shafts, an anchored compliant cup rather than a rigid leaking bearing loop. US-10001245-B2 holds by vacuum and then switches the same pneumatic generator to blower mode to move the assembly on an air cushion, alternating hold and move where this claim requires the hold to persist through sliding contact. US-4934475-A defines its pressure reduction space with a seal member and uses vibration to impart a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering hold, the opposite role vibration plays here. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction plate that lifts sheet articles and sweeps debris with nozzle airflow, cited in the Background for that supported teaching and for saying nothing about holding a vibrating tool on a covering element already bedded. The Background sets out the technical problem the deliberate clearance solves, that sealing demands compliance and compliance in the load path damps the vibration.

The gate failed on brief length: FIG. 1 was 3034 characters against a 2800 maximum. All five briefs are now measured and under the limit.

**FIG. 1, 3034 to 2616 characters.** Shortened by dropping renderer constraints that carried no geometry, not by dropping structure. Removed the repeated "able to hold a point well clear of its boundary lines" from the three blocks, the "no proportion is asserted" restatements where "schematic" already says it, and the "clear of all four of its boundary lines" tails on the endpoint entries, since "well inside its front face" already places a broad interior target. Everything load-bearing is intact: the tile, the slab as base 12 standing on the band, the three blocks side by side on the top face as vibration motor 18, handle 44 and air-extraction mechanism 20, the band meeting the underside and standing on the tile, the schematic and placement-convention disclaimers, and all seven numeral targets including 10 on the upright outline at the left-hand end of the slab, clear of the front face that carries 12.

**FIG. 5, 2874 to 2591 characters.** By `wc` this sheet was also over the limit even though the gate named only FIG. 1, so I trimmed it the same way: compressed the band and cord paragraphs, dropped "away from either of its ends" from numeral 10, and replaced the negative tail on numeral 24 ("not on or below its lower boundary line") with the positive "well inside the front strip of the band, between its upper and lower boundary lines". The cord is still one slack curved path with no attachment formation, and 10 still sits on the machine outline at the right-hand end, clear of the flexible pulling element 46.

**FIG. 2, 2729 to 2693; FIG. 4, 2770 to 2715.** Both were within the limit but with almost no headroom, so I compressed two over-long sentences without touching geometry. FIG. 2 still states that the broken line stops at the upper face and resumes below the lower face with no passage through base 12 drawn or asserted; FIG. 4 still requires hatching continuous beneath the column at an angle different from the band it lies against. FIG. 3 was already short and is untouched.

Numeral coverage is unchanged across the plan, so `draft/numerals.md`, `draft/07-drawings.md`, the detailed description and the claims needed no edit and got none.

FIG. 1 is now 2616 characters. Measuring the other sheets showed FIG. 5 at 2874, also over the limit though unnamed by the gate, so it was trimmed the same way to 2591, and FIG. 2 and FIG. 4, which sat just under the limit, were compressed to 2693 and 2715 for headroom. All five briefs now measure under 2800. Every body, contact, path, schematic disclaimer and numeral target is preserved; no claim, description, drawing description or numeral table entry was touched.
reasoning: The overflow was caused by annotation scaffolding, not by disclosed structure, so I cut only clauses that told the renderer how to draw rather than what exists. The three blocks each carried an identical instruction that their front face be able to hold a point clear of its boundary lines; that requirement is already implicit in an endpoint specified as well inside a face, so one copy of it, let alone three, adds nothing.

Several bodies carried both schematic and no proportion is asserted, which say the same thing twice. Keeping one of the two preserves the source-fidelity guard, which matters because the disclosure gives no dimension or proportion for any part, while halving the words spent on it.

I removed the clear of all four of its boundary lines tails from the endpoint entries for base 12 and handle 44 and the clear of its upper and lower edges tail from perimeter member 24. Well inside its front face is the broad interior target the endpoint guidance asks for and already excludes the edges, so the tails were narrowing language with no distinguishing work to do.

I kept every constraint that distinguishes one part from another visible part. Numeral 10 stays on the upright outline at the left-hand end of the slab and clear of the front face of the slab, because that is what keeps the assembly numeral off the surface whose own endpoint is base 12. In FIG. 4 the exposed face 38 keeps its distinction from covering element 36, and in FIG. 2 the statement that the broken line stops at the upper face and resumes below the lower face, with no passage through base 12 drawn or asserted, is retained because a through-base opening is not disclosed.

Measuring all five sheets rather than only the one named showed FIG. 5 at 2874 characters, over the same limit. Trimming it now avoids handing back a candidate that fails the identical check on the next pass, and the cuts were the same kind: compressed band and cord wording, no change to the single slack curved path, the schematic meeting place with no attachment formation, or the numeral set.

In FIG. 5 I also dropped away from either of its ends from numeral 10 and replaced the negative tail on numeral 24, not on or below its lower boundary line, with the positive statement that the point sits well inside the front strip between its upper and lower boundary lines. That follows the guidance to state required placement positively and to avoid toward-an-end modifiers with no grounding in the disclosure.

Both failing sheets are repaired, and the fixes address the same root cause on each.

**FIG. 4, numerals 26 and 38.** Both parts are faces seen edge on, so the brief defined each target as a single drawn line and the inspectors rejected dots that sat one pixel off it. The endpoints now name the line together with the pixels immediately adjoining it: bearing face 26 is identified at the horizontal line closing the column below, and exposed face 38 at the top boundary line of the uppermost band on the open stretch to the left of the column, in each case with a point touching that line from either side counting as on it. The distinctions that do real work are kept, since 24 is well inside the column's hatching and 36 well inside the band's hatching to the right of the column, so neither face can be confused with the body it bounds. I also replaced the negative tail on 38 ("not in the hatching below it") with that positive tolerance, and added that the two lines bounding the clearance are drawn plainly so there is a line to hit.

**FIG. 5, numeral 24.** The dot fell below the band onto the tile. The band's front strip is now specified as drawn deep, a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below, and the endpoint is stated by the two contacts that bound it: well inside the front strip, above the line along which the band meets the tile and below the line along which it meets the body. The band still stands on the tile with its lower edge meeting it, and the open stretch of tile in front of the machine that carries numeral 36 is unchanged.

**Length.** Adding the tolerance wording pushed FIG. 4 to 2799 characters against the 2800 maximum, so I compressed redundant hatching and schematic phrasing there and in FIG. 5 to restore headroom. All five briefs now measure: FIG. 1 at 2616, FIG. 2 at 2735, FIG. 3 at 2161, FIG. 4 at 2754, FIG. 5 at 2672. I applied the same tolerance clause to first side 14 in FIG. 2, which is the identical edge-on-line target, and paid for it by trimming that sheet's hatching sentence.

The numeral plan is unchanged, so `draft/numerals.md`, `draft/07-drawings.md`, the detailed description and the claims needed no edit and got none.

input.summary: Repaired the two failing sheets. On FIG. 4 the endpoints for bearing face 26 and exposed face 38, both faces seen edge on and therefore defined as single lines, now name the line together with the pixels immediately adjoining it, so a dot touching the line from either side satisfies the specification; the lines bounding the clearance are also required to be drawn plainly. On FIG. 5 the band's front strip is specified as drawn deep, a broad clear surface between the underside of the body and the tile, and numeral 24 is placed well inside that strip, above the line where the band meets the tile and below the line where it meets the body. The added wording took FIG. 4 to one character under the limit, so redundant hatching and schematic phrasing was compressed on FIG. 2, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5; all five briefs now measure between 2161 and 2754 characters. No claim, description, drawing description or numeral table entry was touched.
reasoning: Both FIG. 4 failures share one cause: a face seen edge on is a line, so the brief was demanding a zero-width target and the inspectors rejected dots that landed one pixel into the adjoining hatching. The guidance asks for a broad interior target wherever possible, and where the part genuinely is a line the equivalent is to state that the line together with the pixels immediately touching it is the target. That is what the two entries now say.

I kept the qualifiers that separate a face from the body it bounds, because those are necessary to distinguish the intended part from another visible part: perimeter member 24 is well inside the column's hatching while bearing face 26 is at the line closing that column below, and covering element 36 is well inside the band's hatching to the right of the column while exposed face 38 is at the band's top boundary line on the stretch to the left. Without that separation the tolerance would let a face numeral read as its body.

The negative tail on numeral 38, not in the hatching below it, was removed and replaced by the positive tolerance. It was both a negative linework control and the very thing that made a one-pixel overshoot a failure.

For FIG. 4 I added that the two lines bounding the clearance are drawn plainly. A leader can only terminate on a line the renderer actually draws, and this states the requirement positively rather than banning anything.

The FIG. 5 dot landed below the band on the tile, so I restored the band's front strip as a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below, wording I had compressed away in the previous length repair. Trimming it had removed the reason the strip is deep enough to hold a point.

I restated numeral 24 on FIG. 5 by its two bounding contacts, above the line where the band meets the tile and below the line where it meets the body, rather than by an abstract between the boundary lines. Naming the contacts ties the target to physical relationships already in the sheet instead of to a coordinate.

The tolerance wording is longer than what it replaced, and FIG. 4 landed at 2799 characters against a 2800 maximum, which is no margin at all. I bought headroom by compressing duplicated hatching descriptions and schematic restatements, not by dropping bodies or relationships: hatching is still regularly spaced, parallel, continuous from side to side including beneath the column, and at differing angles on adjoining cut bodies.

First side 14 on FIG. 2 is the same edge-on-line target that just failed twice on FIG. 4, so I gave it the same tolerance clause and paid for the characters by compressing that sheet's hatching sentence. Leaving it as a bare line target would have queued up an identical failure.

While restoring the FIG. 5 band paragraph I checked that the sentence putting the band on the tile survived the rewrite and re-added it, since both the contact and the open stretch of tile in front of the machine carry endpoints for numerals 24 and 36.

Nothing downstream needed synchronizing. Sheet assignments are unchanged at FIG. 1 with 10, 12, 18, 20, 24, 36, 44; FIG. 2 with 12, 14, 20, 22, 24, 36; FIG. 3 with 16, 24; FIG. 4 with 24, 26, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42; FIG. 5 with 10, 24, 36, 46. All 16 table numerals still appear on at least one sheet, none exceeds eight per sheet, and no rendered pixel was allowed to add or alter any structure in the specification or claims.

The negative tail on numeral 38, not in the hatching below it, was removed and replaced by the positive tolerance. It was both a negative linework control and the very thing that made a one-pixel overshoot a failure.

For FIG. 4 I added that the two lines bounding the clearance are drawn plainly. A leader can only terminate on a line the renderer actually draws, and this states the requirement positively rather than banning anything.

The FIG. 5 dot landed below the band on the tile, so I restored the band's front strip as a broad clear surface standing between the underside of the body above and the tile below, wording I had compressed away in the previous length repair. Trimming it had removed the reason the strip is deep enough to hold a point.

I restated numeral 24 on FIG. 5 by its two bounding contacts, above the line where the band meets the tile and below the line where it meets the body, rather than by an abstract between the boundary lines. Naming the contacts ties the target to physical relationships already in the sheet instead of to a coordinate.

US-11408462-B2 forms its peripheral wall from elastic partitions whose end contacts the wall surface and adds a rigid frame member to stop that partition deforming into the decompressed space, teaching the compliant wall this claim excludes from the load path. DE-202021002652-U1 evacuates rubber-elastic aprons on head shells at the ends of motor-vibrated shafts, an anchored compliant cup rather than a rigid leaking bearing loop. US-10001245-B2 holds by vacuum and then switches the same pneumatic generator to blower mode to move the assembly on an air cushion, alternating hold and move where this claim requires the hold to persist through sliding contact. US-4934475-A defines its pressure reduction space with a seal member and uses vibration to impart a lifting force that reduces the suction-adhering hold, the opposite role vibration plays here. US-11247858-B2 is a perforated suction plate that lifts sheet articles and sweeps debris with nozzle airflow, cited in the Background for that supported teaching and for saying nothing about holding a vibrating tool on a covering element already bedded. # FIG. 3 - Bottom plan view of the vibration device

**View:** Plan view looking straight up at the underside of the machine, nothing beneath the machine being drawn. Outline line work only, with no lettering drawn.

**Geometry to be drawn**

The sheet shows the perimeter member 24 as one rectangular ring, and within it the second side 16 as a plain open field; no other body is drawn. The ring is the perimeter member 24 seen end on, shown schematically with a rectangular plan outline, this being a depiction convention for this sheet only.

The ring is drawn as one rectangle with a smaller rectangle inside it, the inner rectangle standing well in from each of the four sides of the outer rectangle. The band lying between the outer rectangle and the inner rectangle is the drawn body. It runs continuously all the way round, turning each of the four corners without interruption, and it is wide along each of its four sides, wide enough for a point well inside it to stand clear of both its outer edge and its inner edge; the width of that band is schematic and no proportion is asserted. The field within the inner rectangle is likewise wide enough for a point well inside it to stand clear of the inner edge all round.

The band carries round each corner as one continuous surface, so that the ring reads as one closed body running between its outer edge and its inner edge.

The field enclosed by the inner rectangle is left entirely open paper.

The ring stands well in from every side of the drawing area, so that the outer rectangle reads plainly as the edge of the ring.

- The perimeter member 24 is the band of the ring, the surface lying between its outer edge and its inner edge. Identified well inside that band along the left-hand side of the ring, in the surface between the outer edge and the inner edge.
- The second side 16 is the underside face that this view looks straight at, and it shows within the perimeter member 24 as the plain field inside the inner edge of the ring. Identified well inside that field, clear of the band all round it.

**Numerals appearing on this figure:** 16, 24

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 16
- 24
